body.heading: Motion into heat
paragraphs: A moving car carries kinetic energy, and stopping means getting rid of it. Brakes do this with friction: when you press the pedal, pads are clamped hard against a spinning metal disc attached to the wheel, and the rubbing converts motion into heat.

Nothing is destroyed — the energy changes form. The disc gets hot, sometimes visibly glowing on racing cars, and the heat flows away into the air. Once the motion energy has become heat, the car has stopped.

body.heading: From pedal to pad
paragraphs: Your foot could never squeeze hard enough directly. The pedal pushes a piston into a cylinder of brake fluid, and the pressure travels through sealed pipes to pistons at each wheel, multiplying the force and clamping the pads evenly.

Most cars use disc brakes at the front, where most of the braking happens as weight pitches forward, and discs or drums at the back. Vented discs — with air channels between two faces — shed heat faster on hard-working front wheels. Simpler drum brakes survive at the back of cheaper cars, where the work is lighter.

body.heading: The square that matters
paragraphs: Kinetic energy grows with the square of speed: a car at 100 kilometres per hour carries four times the energy of the same car at 50. That is why braking distances stretch so sharply as speed rises, and why brakes work hardest on mountain descents and motorways.

If brakes overheat, the pads can glaze and friction falls — a dangerous fading that truck drivers avoid by using low gears on long hills. Electric cars ease the load by braking with their motors, turning some of the energy back into battery charge.

description: Brakes are energy converters: they turn a car's motion into heat through friction, and dump that heat to the air.
